headline: Citizenship is belonging to a place—with rights to participate and responsibilities to contribute
universal_truth: You're not just in a community; you're part of it; belonging includes both receiving and giving
fun_facts: The concept of citizenship originated in ancient Greek city-states
Citizenship involves both legal status and active participation
Studies show civic engagement increases wellbeing and life satisfaction
discussion_questions: What communities are you a citizen of?
How do you participate in your community?
What does good citizenship look like to you?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: You live somewhere. But are you just located there, or are you part of it? Citizenship is more than address—it's belonging. It means you have a stake in what happens and a role in shaping it.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: You could just live in a place without engaging. Why does active citizenship matter?

options.text: Active citizenship creates the community you live in—places improve when people invest; disengagement leaves decisions to others; you get the community you help create
options.response: Yes. Communities aren't given—they're made. By the people who show up, who care, who contribute. Passive residents consume community. Active citizens create it.
Legal status is part of it, but citizenship is also practice—participation, contribution, engagement...

q1.title: Multiple Citizenships
q1.script: You're a citizen of multiple communities simultaneously: neighborhood, city, nation, world. Each level has its own participation opportunities. Engagement at any level matters.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "Multiple Citizenships"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Rights and Duties
q2.script: Citizenship bundles rights (vote, access services) with duties (pay taxes, serve if called). Good citizenship means claiming both sides—receiving benefits and meeting obligations.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Daily Citizenship
q3.script: Citizenship isn't just voting every few years. It's daily practice: knowing neighbors, supporting local, paying attention, speaking up. Small acts aggregate into community quality.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: You're not just in a community; you're part of it. Belonging includes both receiving and giving. Be an active citizen.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 332. Tomorrow, we'll explore people deciding together—democracy. Until then, consider how you participate in your community.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Citizenship Check - How Do You Participate?
growTrack.activity: How do you currently participate in your communities—neighborhood, city, nation? What could you do more? Choose one way to be a more active citizen this week—attend a meeting, help a neighbor, learn about local issues.
